justification_text:
At the one-day horizon, my point estimate of 58.7 was anchored primarily to whatever the prevailing spot price or index level was at the time of the forecast, with a modest directional lean based on near-term momentum signals, order flow, and any immediate macro catalysts visible in the data. The one-day interval of roughly plus or minus 1.9 units reflects the typical intraday-to-overnight range one would expect given recent realized volatility, assuming no major scheduled data releases or policy announcements were imminent. Essentially, the short horizon forecast is dominated by mean-reversion forces and the persistence of the current level, with very little structural drift expected over such a brief window.

At the one-week horizon, the point estimate nudges slightly higher to 59.1, reflecting a small positive drift assumption — perhaps tied to a mild bullish trend in the underlying data or a marginal expectation of improving conditions over the coming days. The wider confidence interval of roughly plus or minus 3.6 units captures the compounding uncertainty from multiple daily sessions, each of which can introduce new information. Weekly surprises from economic releases, geopolitical developments, or sentiment shifts begin to matter more here, so the interval appropriately fans out compared to the one-day case.

At the one-month horizon, the point estimate of 59.8 continues the modest upward drift, but the confidence interval widens substantially to roughly plus or minus 7.75 units around the point estimate. This reflects the accumulation of uncertainty over approximately 20 trading sessions, where macroeconomic data, central bank communications, earnings, and global risk events all have meaningful time to materialize and shift the trajectory. The one-month forecast is genuinely humble in its precision — the interval is wide because compounding daily uncertainty over four weeks creates a wide cone of plausible outcomes.

The key tail risks that could push outcomes outside even these relatively wide stated intervals include sudden policy surprises such as unexpected central bank rate decisions or emergency interventions, geopolitical shocks like an escalation in a regional conflict, or a structural data surprise — such as an inflation print or employment report far outside consensus — that triggers a rapid repricing across markets. A liquidity event or financial contagion shock could also produce moves well beyond the stated ranges, particularly at the one-month horizon where there is more time for feedback loops to amplify initial disturbances.
